key_terms.meaning: The smooth curve into which the centroidal axis of a beam bends under load, described by y(x).
Product of Young's modulus E (N/m²) and second moment of area I (m⁴), in N·m²; it measures resistance to bending curvature.
1/ρ = M/EI, where ρ is the radius of curvature (m) and M is the bending moment (N·m) at that section.
Known values of deflection or slope at a support (y = 0 at a simple support; y = 0 and dy/dx = 0 at a fixed end) used to find constants of integration.
Integrating EI y″ = M twice gives EI y′ = ∫M dx + C₁ and EI y = ∫∫M dx dx + C₁x + C₂.
The term ⟨x − a⟩ⁿ, which equals zero while x < a and equals (x − a)ⁿ once x ≥ a.
One moment expression written for the whole beam with bracket terms, so that two constants serve the entire beam.
The bending moment diagram of the beam with every ordinate divided by EI; its area has units of slope (radians).
The vertical distance of a point on the elastic curve from the tangent drawn at another point, equal to the first moment of the M/EI area between them.

A fictitious beam of the same length whose loading is the M/EI diagram of the real beam and whose support conditions are chosen so that its shear equals real slope and its moment equals real deflection.
In a linear elastic beam the slope or deflection due to several loads equals the algebraic sum of the values produced by each load acting alone.
U = ∫ M²/(2EI) dx over the length (J), the elastic energy stored in a beam by bending.
The partial derivative of total strain energy with respect to a load gives the deflection at that load in its own direction: δ = ∂U/∂P.
Deflection = ∫ M m/(EI) dx, where M is the moment from real loads and m is the moment from a unit load at the point and direction wanted.
For a linear elastic beam, deflection at point 1 due to a unit load at point 2 equals deflection at point 2 due to a unit load at point 1.
Work done by system A through the displacements of system B equals the work done by B through the displacements of A.
A support reaction beyond the number needed for static equilibrium, found from compatibility rather than from force and moment balance.
The condition that deflection at a support equals the support's known settlement, written to solve for the redundant reaction.
A cantilever with one extra simple support at the free end; statically indeterminate to the first degree.
A relation linking the bending moments at three consecutive supports of a continuous beam, including settlement terms.

takeaways: The elastic curve obeys EI d²y/dx² = M, so bending moment and curvature are the same story told in different units.
Double integration is the base method; every other method is a shortcut for the constants C₁ and C₂.
Macaulay's brackets let one moment equation describe a beam with many loads, which saves algebra but demands careful sign handling.
The moment-area theorems convert an integral into an area and a first moment, which is fast for one or two deflections.
The conjugate beam turns slope and deflection into shear and moment, so a beam you already know solves a problem you do not.
Superposition works only while the material is linear elastic and deflections stay small enough not to change the load geometry.
Energy methods give the deflection at a chosen point directly, without ever finding the full elastic curve.
In an indeterminate beam, the extra support is removed to get a determinate base beam, and compatibility of deflection supplies the missing equation.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for a full worked derivation of slope and deflection for a given beam plus a sketch of the elastic curve, and the indeterminate questions expect the redundant reaction first, then the bending moment diagram.

bank.q: Derive the differential equation of the elastic curve of a straight beam and state the sign convention used for sagging and hogging.
outline: Draw a small element of the bent beam and mark the strain variation across the depth
Relate fibre strain to curvature: ε = y/ρ
Apply Hooke's law to get stress, then integrate stress over the section to get M
Result EI/ρ = M, and for small slopes 1/ρ ≈ d²y/dx²
State sign convention: sagging moment positive, upward deflection positive

bank.q: State the two moment-area theorems and explain what each one gives physically, with a sketch of an M/EI diagram.
outline: First theorem: angle between tangents at A and B equals area of M/EI diagram between A and B
Second theorem: tangential deviation of B from tangent at A equals first moment of that area about B
Explain units of each quantity
Sketch a typical M/EI diagram and show the area and the centroid distance

bank.q: Explain the conjugate beam method. Give the mapping of real supports to conjugate supports and explain why shear gives slope and moment gives deflection.
outline: Define the conjugate beam: same length, loaded with the M/EI diagram
State the four standard support mappings: simple–simple, fixed–free, free–fixed, fixed–fixed
Show that the conjugate shear equals slope and conjugate moment equals deflection
Explain the need for real beams that are stable; a determinate real beam gives a stable conjugate beam
Work a small example, for instance slope at the support of a simply supported beam

bank.q: State Maxwell's reciprocal theorem and prove it from Betti's theorem for a linear elastic beam.
outline: State Betti's theorem in words with work terms
Apply unit load at 1 first, then at 2, and equal the total work in both orders
Cancel the second-order term to obtain δ₁₂ = δ₂₁
Give one practical use, such as influence lines or checking a computed deflection matrix

bank.q: Explain the principle of superposition and list the conditions under which it is valid for beam deflections.
outline: State that response to several loads is the sum of responses to individual loads
Validity needs linear elasticity (stress proportional to strain)
Small deflections, so the load position and arm do not change
No yielding, no buckling, no change of geometry
Give a two-load cantilever example

bank.q: A simply supported beam of span L carries a uniformly distributed load w per unit length over its whole span. Using the double integration method, find the maximum deflection and the slope at the supports.
outline: Write M(x) = wLx/2 − wx²/2
Integrate twice with EI
Apply y = 0 at x = 0 and x = L to fix C₁ and C₂
Get slope at support = wL³/24EI
Get maximum deflection at midspan = 5wL⁴/384EI
State the direction of deflection and check symmetry

bank.q: Use Macaulay's method to find the deflection under the point loads on a simply supported beam of span 6 m carrying 20 kN at 2 m and 30 kN at 4 m from the left support.
outline: Find reactions from moment balance
Write a single moment equation with bracket terms for both loads
Integrate twice and keep brackets intact throughout
Apply y = 0 at both supports
Get both constants and substitute the required x values
State deflections in mm with direction

bank.q: A cantilever of length L carries a point load W at its free end. Find the slope and deflection at the free end by the moment-area method and by the conjugate beam method, and check that the answers agree.
outline: Draw M/EI diagram: triangle of peak value WL/EI at the fixed end
Moment-area: slope at free end = area = WL²/2EI
Deflection = first moment about the free end = WL³/3EI
Conjugate beam: free end becomes fixed, fixed end becomes free
Conjugate shear at free end gives slope, conjugate moment gives deflection
Compare the two results

bank.q: A propped cantilever of span L carries a uniformly distributed load w over its whole length. Find the prop reaction using the method of superposition and then draw the bending moment diagram.
outline: Remove the prop: cantilever with UDL, downward deflection at free end = wL⁴/8EI
Apply upward prop force R alone: upward deflection = RL³/3EI
Compatibility: net deflection at prop is zero, so R = 3wL/8
Find fixed end moment from statics: wL²/8 − RL
Locate the point of contraflexure and the maximum sagging moment

bank.q: Using Castigliano's theorem, find the deflection at the free end of a cantilever of length L carrying a uniformly distributed load w.
outline: Write M(x) = w(L − x)²/2 or an equivalent form
Add a dummy point load P at the free end if a general expression is wanted
Write U = ∫ M²/(2EI) dx
Differentiate under the integral sign with respect to P
Set P = 0 and evaluate the integral to get wL⁴/8EI
Comment on why energy methods avoid finding the full elastic curve

bank.q: A simply supported beam of span L carries a central point load W. Using the conjugate beam method find the slope at the supports and the deflection at midspan.
outline: M/EI diagram is a triangle with peak WL/4EI at midspan
Conjugate beam is simply supported with the same span
Reaction of conjugate beam equals slope at real support
Reaction = (1/2)(WL/4EI)(L/2) = WL²/16EI
Conjugate moment at midspan gives deflection WL³/48EI

bank.q: A fixed beam of span L carries a central point load W. Analyse it by Macaulay's method to get the fixed end moments, the deflection at midspan and the position of maximum deflection.
outline: Use symmetry: vertical reactions W/2 each
Write one moment equation with an unknown fixed end moment M_F
Integrate twice and apply slope zero and deflection zero at both ends
Solve for M_F = WL/8, hogging at both ends
Deflection at midspan = WL³/192EI
Show maximum deflection occurs at midspan by symmetry

bank.q: A continuous beam has three supports A, B and C with spans L₁ and L₂, carrying uniformly distributed loads w₁ and w₂. Support B settles by δ. Derive and apply Clapeyron's theorem of three moments to find the support moments.
outline: Write the three-moment equation including the settlement term 6EIδ/L
Substitute M_A = M_C = 0 for simple end supports
Solve for M_B
Find reactions by taking moments about B for each span
Sketch the bending moment diagram and mark hogging over B
Explain how settlement changes the moments even with no load pattern change

bank.q: Compare the double integration, Macaulay, moment-area and conjugate beam methods for a beam with three point loads. Discuss accuracy, effort and the type of beam each suits best.
outline: Double integration: needs one equation per segment, many constants
Macaulay: one equation, brackets handle discontinuities
Moment-area: good for one or two deflections, area computation can be tedious
Conjugate beam: needs a stable conjugate, fast for standard cases
All four give identical results for a linear elastic beam
Recommend a method for the given load pattern and say why

bank.q: A simply supported beam of span 8 m carries a point load of 40 kN at midspan. The support at one end settles by 5 mm. Evaluate the effect on the midspan bending moment and deflection, taking EI = 20 000 kN·m², and comment on the result.
outline: Compute the load-only midspan moment and deflection
Add the effect of settlement as a rigid body rotation producing a moment
Show that settlement increases or decreases deflection depending on the direction
Conclude that support movement changes moments in indeterminate beams but only changes geometry in a determinate simply supported beam
State the practical warning for structures on soft soil

bank.q: Derive the expression for strain energy stored in a beam due to bending and use it, with the unit load method, to obtain the deflection at the free end of a cantilever carrying a point load at the free end.
outline: Start from U = ∫ M²/(2EI) dx and explain each term
Write real moment M = W(L − x)
Write unit-load moment m = 1·(L − x)
Apply δ = ∫ M m/(EI) dx
Integrate from 0 to L to get WL³/3EI
Note that the unit load method is a statement of the principle of virtual work

glossary.def: The vertical displacement of a point on the axis of a beam measured from its unloaded position, in metres or millimetres.
The angle the tangent to the elastic curve makes with the original axis, in radians, equal to dy/dx.
A bending moment that curves the beam concave upward, producing compression at the top and tension at the bottom.
A bending moment that curves the beam concave downward, producing tension at the top and compression at the bottom.
The radius ρ of the circular arc that best fits the elastic curve at a section; equals EI/M.
The geometric property I of a cross-section about its bending axis, in m⁴, which resists bending.
The ratio of direct stress to direct strain in the linear elastic range, in N/m².
A beam whose support reactions can all be found from static equilibrium alone.
A beam with more unknown reactions than equilibrium equations, so compatibility of deformation is also needed.
The number of extra unknown reactions beyond the available equilibrium equations.
A fictitious load applied at a point where no real load acts, so that Castigliano's theorem yields the deflection there; set to zero after differentiation.
A point where the bending moment changes sign, so the curvature reverses and the elastic curve has an inflection.
The bending moment that develops at a built-in end of a beam when rotation there is prevented.
A beam fixed at one end and simply supported at the other, indeterminate to the first degree.
A single beam running over three or more supports, so the intermediate moments are statically indeterminate.
A reaction or internal force chosen as the unknown to be removed, solved for, and then restored.
The principle that external work done by a virtual unit load equals internal work, the basis of the unit load method.
A material response in which stress is proportional to strain and all deformation disappears on unloading.
The assumption that slopes are small enough for (dy/dx)² to be neglected compared with 1, so curvature ≈ d²y/dx².
The load per unit deflection at a chosen point, in N/m, equal to the reciprocal of the flexibility there.
The deflection at one point due to a unit load at another point; Maxwell's theorem says the matrix of these is symmetric.
Downward movement of a support, which enters an indeterminate analysis as a known non-zero deflection at that support.
A beam made of stacked curved plates, analysed as a cantilever or simply supported beam in bending, common in older vehicle suspension.
An equation relating the moments at three successive supports of a continuous beam to the loads, spans and settlements.
